manager.visualize()
Explain 4C — manager and connection

manager = CodeAgent(...) creates another object with its own execution history. cargo_time and save_report are supplied function tools: register their names without calling them here. managed_agents=[specialist] gives this manager access to the first agent. visualize() prints the configured tree; it does not demonstrate an actual delegation. The manager waits for the specialist to return; this example does not run both agents in parallel.

Check C: draw the tree from your code before running it. Which agent can search, which can save, and what line would break delegation if removed?

Build answer C

Manager → cargo_time, save_report, and web specialist → web_search, visit_webpage. The framework may also show final_answer. Removing managed_agents=[specialist] removes the manager's delegation connection.

docs.title: 4D. Add the tasks only after both agents exist
docs.text:
Append this last block at the bottom of the same file. Start with ONE_LOCATION_TASK, which checks one filming claim. TASK contains the four-location research request for step 6.

my_batman.py
TASK = """Alfred needs three Batman filming locations and one supercar factory.
Use at most FOUR separate web_specialist calls, ONE named candidate per call:
Wollaton Hall, Knebworth House, Mentmore Towers, and Lamborghini Sant'Agata Bolognese.
Use ONE delegation per manager action step; do not combine delegations in a loop.
These are candidates to VERIFY, not facts to assume. For each, request a supported
filming/factory claim, coordinates, source_url, coordinate_source_url and a short
evidence quote. Ask the specialist to use focused page excerpts, at most one search
and three page attempts, and return one compact record under 500 characters.
Preserve each record before the next delegation. Do not request all four places
in one specialist call. Do not repeat a failed delegation or invent missing data.
If four supported rows are unavailable, report the gaps without saving a complete report.
Otherwise calculate all four cargo estimates and call save_report in ONE Python
action using the compact rows; do not print the whole JSON again. Then finish with
the report path, sources and assumptions. Keep responses and printed output short.
"""

ONE_LOCATION_TASK = """Delegate ONCE to web_specialist: check ONLY whether
Wollaton Hall was used as Wayne Manor in a Batman film. First read
https://wollatonhall.org.uk/hall-and-museum/history/ with focus="Wayne Manor Batman".
If blocked or insufficient, use at most one search and one alternate page.
Stop as soon as a relevant page supports the claim. Do NOT research coordinates,
transport, opening times or other places. Return the claim, source URL, one short
quote and uncertainty in at most 500 characters. If unsupported, mark it missing.
The manager should preserve that evidence and finish. No calculation or report.
"""

run_task(manager, ONE_LOCATION_TASK)
Explain 4D — construction versus execution

Triple-quoted text stores each task as one multi-line string. Defining TASK does not run it. run_task(manager, ONE_LOCATION_TASK) starts the manager's model/action/observation loop using the smaller request. The manager may then call the separately created specialist. That specialist has its own loop and must return its evidence.

Check D: which line starts model reasoning, and does the tree prove the specialist has been called?

Build answer D

run_task(manager, ONE_LOCATION_TASK) starts the task loop. The tree proves only configuration; the trace must show an actual web_specialist(task=...) call.

Before running: your file should now have one import/model section, one specialist constructor, one manager constructor, the two tasks and one run_task call. Explain the two constructors and the connecting line to a partner or in evidence.md; then save and continue below.

docs.title: 5. Test one filming claim
docs.text:
For the first run, check only the filming claim. Leave coordinate research for step 6. Check the returned quote against its source.

Enforced limit First run Manager action steps 3 Specialist action steps 4 per delegation Search attempts 1 per delegation, at most 2 short results Page attempts 2 per delegation, including failures; no repeat URL Page excerpt / printed observation At most 1,600 / 1,800 characters Model output allowance 800 tokens per response; this is not an input-token limit

These are limits, not a required step count. A failed task may make one extra framework final-answer request at its step limit. A page refusal or exhausted research budget should lead to a short incomplete answer, not more retries.

After saving steps 4A–4D, check that the last line is run_task(manager, ONE_LOCATION_TASK).

Run: python my_batman.py. Enter your Groq key if prompted. The code first prints the tree, then the manager should delegate the supplied Wollaton Hall task to the specialist.

What to check: copy a short actual trace excerpt into Topic 15 → One-location handoff in your existing evidence.md:

Stage Find this in your own run Manager action An executed web_specialist(task=...) request. Specialist action Its page-reading call and any permitted search fallback. A successful first source needs no search. Observation A returned page passage or an explicit retrieval failure. Specialist return The filming claim, source URL, short quote and uncertainty. Coordinates are not requested in this test. Manager response Whether it preserves the source and limitation.

1. Is this the same as the manager calling web_search directly?

Answer 1 — two loops

No. The manager calls web_specialist, which has its own loop and may make several tool calls before returning. web_search is a function-like tool action inside that specialist's loop.

2. Should this small test create outputs/batman-report.html?

Answer 2 — small-test output

No. The supplied one-location task explicitly requests no calculation or report. Its result is in the terminal. The report is generated only in the full-task step below; do not create an empty HTML file yourself.

3. What if the manager never delegates, a page fails, or the run reaches its limit?

Answer 3 — an incomplete run

Record the actual failure and mark this run incomplete. A final answer alone is insufficient. Check the four build stages, both agent constructors, the managed-agent connection and the direct tools. Keep the limits; record the failure rather than repeatedly retrying. Use the research-limit guidance to decide what to check next.

docs.title: 6. Research four locations and inspect the report
docs.text:
The full task covers three filming sites and one factory, but uses one place per specialist delegation. Each call starts a fresh specialist history, so whole pages from the earlier location do not accumulate there. The manager retains only the compact returned records.

In the existing my_batman.py, make these changes, then save:

  1. Change ResearchBudget(max_searches=1, max_pages=2) to ResearchBudget(max_searches=1, max_pages=3). This allows a claim page, a coordinate page and at most one alternate.
  2. In the specialist constructor, change agent_options(max_steps=4, compact=True) to agent_options(max_steps=5, compact=True).
  3. In the manager constructor, change agent_options(max_steps=3, compact=True) to agent_options(max_steps=6, compact=True).
  4. Change the final call from run_task(manager, ONE_LOCATION_TASK) to run_task(manager, TASK).

Keep the excerpt, print and model-output caps. Do not raise limits to force a complete report. The task requests at most four short delegations, then combined calculation/report writing and a final answer. If a claim or coordinate cannot be supported within the budget, an honest gap is the expected result.

What to inspect: each web_specialist(task=...) should name only one place, in a separate manager action step. Its step counter starts again for that task. The manager should keep each source-backed record and should not ask a new specialist run to rediscover an earlier result. Printing all four handoffs in one action could clip the last record, so keep each delegation in a separate step.

Run: python my_batman.py. Check the terminal trace. If save_report succeeded, it creates outputs/batman-report.html inside week04-exercises. In File Explorer/Finder, open week04-exercises → outputs and double-click batman-report.html to view it in your browser. If the file is missing, look for the save_report call and any error in the terminal.

Copy the generated HTML in your file manager into the existing evidence-files folder, keeping its name batman-report.html. This is a copy of an output, not a new program. Paste the actual sources/trace into evidence.md. The report writer recalculates hours and writes a table and coordinate plot. It checks basic input shape/URLs, not whether a webpage supports the claim. Check every source and coordinate even if the report file was created successfully.

Open the full-size original

Original example output, unchanged: Hugging Face Multi-Agent Systems. Use it to discuss marker position, color, labels and evidence; it is not an answer key for your research.

How final checks differ from another agent: smolagents can run Python final_answer_checks before accepting an answer. A check can reject missing output or inconsistent data, but that callback is not automatically a third agent. Here, you check the sources and map yourself. In the optional challenge, you add another agent to check a researched record. Compare the evidence each type of check can examine.

Your classroom output uses a lightweight longitude/latitude coordinate plot without a geographic basemap. Check the printed legend: purple means under five estimated hours; red means five or more. A neat visual can still hide wrong coordinates, overlapping locations or unsupported film associations.

Check your map: choose one marker, locate the corresponding row, check both source URLs, and recompute its time. Would a longitude-sign error move it to the other side of the map? Does the color agree with the estimate? Note one limitation of this simplified map and one limitation of the flight assumption.

Map answer 1 — location and longitude sign

Check the marker's name against the row and both source pages. Changing the sign of longitude reflects its horizontal position across the zero-longitude line; for a western location it can place the marker far to the east. A plausible-looking marker does not verify the source coordinate.

Map answer 2 — time and color

Recompute round(distance_km * 1.1 / 750 + 1, 2) with a source-backed destination. Under the printed legend, values below five hours are purple and values of five or more are red. An unrelated color or unsupported coordinate needs correction.

Map answer 3 — limits and final checks

The coordinate plot has no geographic basemap and can overlap markers; the flight estimate ignores real routing, schedules and handling constraints. A Python final-answer check can test a file or data rule. A verifier agent has its own model/tool loop and must show which sources it checked. Neither proves that a claim is correct without suitable evidence.

docs.title: 7. Check and explain the team you built
docs.text:
Check your results: use your report and terminal output to answer the questions below in evidence.md.

1. Does every row have a supported role and coordinate? Open both source links for each of the three filming sites and one factory. Write one supported example and any gap you find.

Answer 1 — check the evidence

A claim source must support the film/factory role; a coordinate source must establish the location used in the calculation. A working URL or plausible number alone is not enough. Record gaps honestly; do not label an unsupported four-row report complete.

2. Where do the model decisions end and the supplied Python tool's work begin?

Answer 2 — model and tool responsibilities

Groq produces the actions and report reasoning. Local Python runs search/page requests and the supplied calculator/report writer. cargo_time calculates from input coordinates; it does not discover or verify them. save_report renders the given rows; it does not prove that a cited page supports a claim.

3. Would one agent always be worse than this team?

Answer 3 — team trade-off

No. One agent may be simpler for a small task. A team separates responsibilities and histories, but adds calls, coordination and possible handoff losses. Judge actual supported results, not the number of agents.

Checkpoint: keep the two required Python files, the one-location trace, the full-run trace, checked source links, one recalculated estimate and your understanding answers in the existing evidence note. Keep the generated report and its archive copy if the full task succeeded. If a run failed, keep the error message and note which checks remain incomplete.

docs.title: If the service refuses a request
docs.text:
• Page 403: the website blocked the request. It counts as an attempt; use one permitted alternate or mark the source unavailable. Do not retry the blocked URL.
  • Research limit reached: return the evidence collected and identify missing fields. A refusal does not prove a fact is false.
  • Groq 413 / request too large: stop that run. Check that your helper files match the latest download and that you are using ONE_LOCATION_TASK; start a fresh small run after correcting it. Waiting alone does not shrink a large history.
  • Groq 429: the shared model in 4A spaces requests and allows at most two extra 429 attempts across the run. If it stops, inspect account limits and the service’s retry interval. Do not immediately restart. Waiting does not replenish credits or guarantee success; daily/token limits or billing issues may require later capacity or account action.

See Groq’s rate-limit explanation. A local character cap is not an exact token count. Do not paste a whole page into the task or increase the step limits to work around a service refusal.

docs.title: 8. Optional challenge: add a verifier agent
docs.text:
Add a third agent that independently checks one result from your Batman research. Complete the two-agent exercise first, then save a copy for this challenge:

  1. Open your working, saved my_batman.py in the editor.
  2. Choose File → Save As and save a copy as my_batman_verified.py directly in week04-exercises. Keep my_batman.py as the two-agent version.
  3. Confirm that both filenames appear in the editor's file list, and that you are now editing my_batman_verified.py. This file is not supplied in the ZIP.
  4. In the copied file, you create the verifier after the specialist = CodeAgent(...) block and before manager = CodeAgent(...). Register both with the manager; keep the same model connection. Keep the changes in this copied file.
  5. Replace the copied file's TASK with your own one-row research and verification request, using one entry from the existing report as a candidate to recheck. Request both delegations and a sourced verdict, without saving another report. Keep each specialist at four steps, with its own one-search/two-page budget. Give the copied manager four steps. Confirm its last call uses your new TASK, then save. Use the hints below if you get stuck.

What this file does — my_batman_verified.py: your copied and edited Groq program adds an independent checking loop for one candidate row. It uses live research tools and prints both handoffs/verdicts in the terminal. Compare with your existing report; this bounded optional test does not overwrite it. Checking all four rows would require separate fresh one-row runs, rather than packing eight delegations into the six-step required full task.

Before adding the verifier, decide:

  1. Give it a distinct name, a description and a narrow checking responsibility. Decide which tools it needs and why it must read the cited pages independently.
  2. Define a verdict format with pass, fail or uncertain for each row, plus the checked URL, supported/disputed claim, and correction or missing evidence. State what makes a verdict credible.
  3. Decide when the manager should call the verifier and what the manager should do with each verdict. Who can author the report? Who can block an unsupported row?
  4. Add a new CodeAgent object. Register it alongside the web specialist in the manager's managed_agents list. Update the manager task so the one sourced record reaches the verifier before the manager accepts it.
  5. Inspect the tree: it should have a manager and two different specialists. Then inspect execution: both specialist calls must actually occur.

Challenge test: in this same optional file, first copy your normal final call into evidence.md. Temporarily replace its final call with run_task(manager, "YOUR FALSE-CLAIM TEST REQUEST")—no new test file is needed. In your request, supply one deliberately wrong label, such as “Wollaton Hall is a supercar factory,” and the official hall history source. Ask for a verdict without saving a report. Predict the result, then inspect whether the verifier reads the page and rejects or marks the claim uncertain. Label the claim as an intentional test error in your evidence; do not submit it as a research result.

Optional run: save and run python my_batman_verified.py for the false-claim test, then restore run_task(manager, TASK), save and rerun your one-row research/verification task. Keep both results under Topic 15 → Optional verifier in your existing evidence.md. Compare with the existing two-agent report: did the new agent catch the injected error? Did it supply a checked source or merely repeat the researcher's wording? Record added model calls and any remaining uncertainty.

Hint 1 — create a different agent

Give the verifier its own name, description and CodeAgent object. Assigning the existing specialist to a second variable does not create a new loop.

Hint 2 — connect the new agent

Use managed_agents=[specialist, verifier] on the copied manager. Give the verifier its own ResearchBudget(max_searches=1, max_pages=2), bounded search/page tools and at most four steps. Bind that budget to the verifier; do not share its counters with the researcher or give it the report-writing tool. Check one row per delegation and keep verdicts short.

Hint 3 — request verification

Registration is not execution. Update the manager task to hand over the sourced row and request a verdict. Specify what happens after fail or uncertain; this bounded extension does not save a new report.

Verifier answer 1 — name, scope and tools

A suitable role is an independent claim/coordinate checker, with its own name and page-reading/search tools. It should inspect the cited source rather than trust the researcher's confidence.

Verifier answer 2 — a useful verdict

Return pass/fail/uncertain for each claim, checked URL, the evidence, and a correction or missing field. A verdict without an inspected source is only another assertion.

Verifier answer 3 — when to accept a row

Call the verifier after research and before accepting the row. Return an evidence-backed verdict or honest uncertainty; do not start repair loops after the budget is exhausted. This test leaves the existing report unchanged. In a later reporting workflow, only the manager would write a verified report.

Verifier answer 4 — expected configuration and execution

The tree contains the manager plus two distinct specialists. The trace must then show the manager calling both specialists; the tree alone does not prove either call happened.

Verifier answer 5 — false-claim test

A hall's filming/history page does not establish that it is a supercar factory. After reading the source, a verifier should reject that factory claim or mark it unsupported/uncertain. Record the actual result if it misses the error. Then restore your normal one-row task and compare the verdicts; an extra agent does not guarantee a useful correction.

What counts as the extension?

A third object in a diagram is insufficient. Show the new design, the actual second delegation, a page observation, and a verdict linked to evidence. An independent checker may still be wrong; you still need to check its sources.

docs.title: Explain the system
docs.text:
Write your own answers 1–5 under Topic 17 in your existing evidence.md, then expand the answers to compare. Use one short example from your actual run wherever possible.

1. Why is delegating to an agent different from calling a function tool?

Answer 1 — another execution loop

A function tool executes its specified Python operation and returns a value/error. A specialist agent has its own model/action/observation loop and may choose several searches/page reads before returning a report. Show the manager's specialist call and one specialist tool action from your run.

2. What information must the specialist return to the manager?

Answer 2 — information to return

The location and role, coordinates, claim source URL, coordinate source URL, supporting evidence and uncertainty must remain available. Without them, the manager cannot calculate the estimate or check the report. In your trace, identify the returned fields rather than assuming they survived.

3. Why does successful retrieval not establish every requested fact?

Answer 3 — returned passages versus support

Retrieval ranks candidate passages; they may be irrelevant or lack the requested fact. The Week 3 top-five search can return all five notes despite no allergy policy being present. The answer should state that the supplied notes do not establish the policy, not invent one or claim no real policy exists.

4. How does images=[image] differ from a screenshot callback?

Answer 4 — initial input versus new observation

images=[image] supplies pixels at the start of the task. The callback captures the browser after an action and attaches fresh pixels to an action-step observation for a later model call. A saved PNG alone is not evidence that the model received it. Match one changed screenshot to the next answer in your run.

5. What could make a larger team less useful than a single agent?

Answer 5 — coordination costs and errors

Extra calls, latency, lost sources, unclear responsibility and repeated unsupported assertions can outweigh specialization. A verifier is useful only when its checks add evidence or catch a problem. More agents and agreement do not guarantee correctness.

Final checkpoint: keep the supplied helpers, your five my_*.py programs, existing evidence note, generated assets/results and archived comparisons together in week04-exercises. Include my_batman_verified.py if you attempted the optional challenge. Be ready to open a named file, point to an actual action/observation and explain one limitation.

docs.title: Local settings: create .env
docs.text:
In your editor, create .env beside week04_common.py inside week04-exercises. Save it as .env, not .env.txt. Paste these two lines and replace only the key placeholder with your own key:

GROQ_API_KEY=your_own_groq_api_key
GROQ_MODEL=qwen/qwen3.8-27b

Keep this file on your computer. Never upload it to GitHub, add it to evidence, or show it in screenshots. The model ID is listed in Groq’s supported models (checked 2026-11-04); it is a preview model, so check that page and your account access if it changes. Use the plain ID here, without an extra groq/ prefix.

Creating .env alone does not load it into Python. Step 4A of the Batman lesson calls load_dotenv(Path(__file__).with_name(".env"), override=False) before reading the settings. Existing terminal environment values take priority; remove an old terminal value or open a fresh terminal if it selects the wrong model/key. Do not print the key to check it.

The supplied week04_common.py does not read .env: it checks the terminal environment, then asks for the key with hidden input, and uses a fixed model ID. Leave that helper unchanged. The Batman code below replaces only its model construction in your own my_batman.py, keeps hidden input as a fallback when the key is absent, and reads GROQ_MODEL. For Topic 16, the unchanged examples still use the supplied helper and its hidden-key prompt/fixed model; a .env file alone does not change them.

Install the additions after the ZIP requirements, in the activated terminal above:

python -m pip install "smolagents[litellm]==1.13.0" "ddgs==9.16.0" "python-dotenv>=1.0,<2"
python -m pip check

This adds support for the current search wrapper, .env loading and LiteLLM integration while keeping the course’s smolagents version. If you cloned the GitHub repository instead of using the ZIP, run python -m pip install -r requirements.txt from the repository root; that root list includes the Week 4 starter list and these additions. The ZIP’s requirements.txt is a different file and stays unchanged. Continue reading these online pages for the updated steps; the lessons inside the unchanged ZIP are older.

docs.text:
Create a text file named evidence.md to keep your predictions, answers and short excerpts from your results. Markdown is plain text, so you can use your code editor. The file is not included in the ZIP and is not a Python program.

  1. In your editor, choose File → New Text File.
  2. Paste the starter headings below.
  3. Choose File → Save As and save it as evidence.md directly inside week04-exercises, beside requirements.txt.
  4. Save with Ctrl + S or Command + S. Confirm the filename is evidence.md, not evidence.md.txt.
  5. In the editor's file list or your file manager, choose New Folder and create evidence-files inside week04-exercises. Use this folder to keep copies of reports and screenshots for comparison.

docs.title: 14 · Check your Week 3 RAG understanding
docs.text:
Quick recap: RAG retrieves relevant passages so the model can answer from evidence. Agentic RAG lets the agent choose when and what to retrieve. Check the source; say when evidence is missing.

Objective: check whether an answer is supported by retrieved text.

Return to Week 3 for the practical

If you have not done the RAG practical, return to 12 · Building Agentic RAG Systems and follow its existing setup, file-creation and run instructions in First_agent_template. If you already did it, review your saved code and trace. 13 · Week 3 completion checks lists the earlier files. Do not recreate them in week04-exercises or install RAG packages in the Week 4 environment.

Answer the questions using your Week 3 results or the provided example below. Label your notes “Week 3 run” or “provided example” so you can tell which evidence you used. You do not need a new Python program for this review.

Where to write: open the existing evidence.md you created in Week 4 setup, under Topic 14 — Week 3 RAG review. Write your answers in that file.

docs.title: What is BM25?
docs.text:
BM25 ranks documents using keyword matches. It considers how often query words occur, how distinctive they are across the collection, and document length; repeated matches have diminishing benefit. It retrieves candidate passages; it does not generate an answer or verify a claim.

In the Week 3 example BM25 searches five local party notes, without an LLM, embeddings or a vector database. The model separately chooses a query and writes an answer from the returned observations. The tool requests up to five results from five short notes, so it can return notes even when none contains the requested fact. A high rank is not proof that an answer exists, and keyword matching does not automatically resolve synonyms.

Reference: BM25 scoring and normalization. No formula is required for this review.

docs.title: Read the evidence
docs.text:
Read this example; do not paste it into a Python file or run it. It shows the main steps of the Week 3 retrieval loop. Your own tool output may contain several notes.

Task: Suggest a superhero dish and cite its source.
Agent action: party_planning_retriever(query="superhero catering")
Tool observation:
  For catering, serve dishes named after superheroes, like
  'The Hulk's Green Smoothie' and 'Iron Man's Power Steak.'
  Source: Catering Ideas
Final answer: Try The Hulk's Green Smoothie [Catering Ideas].

Second query: caterer allergy policy
Observation: the five party notes contain no allergy policy.

docs.title: Compare and check understanding
docs.text:
Try each question before opening its answer. Quote the action, passage and source from either your Week 3 results or the provided example.

1. Underline the passage and source label supporting the suggested dish. What does that passage establish?

Answer 1 — passage and source

Mark “The Hulk's Green Smoothie” in the catering passage and Source: Catering Ideas. They support the dish suggestion, not ingredients or allergy handling. In your note, use bold text or quote the exact words.

2. Which line demonstrates agent retrieval? How does it differ from a direct Python tool check?

Answer 2 — an executed retrieval action

The agent action party_planning_retriever(query="superhero catering"), followed by its returned passage, demonstrates retrieval in the loop. A direct tool test alone does not show the model chose a retrieval action. Matching the final claim to the passage shows available support; it cannot prove the model used no prior knowledge.

3. For the second query, do the notes contain an allergy policy? Why might BM25 still return results?

Answer 3 — missing evidence

No. Ranking the top five notes does not require any note to contain a policy. Say “The supplied notes do not provide the caterer's allergy policy.” This does not establish that the caterer has no policy.

4. Rewrite this unsupported answer: “The caterer guarantees a nut-free menu and checks every guest's allergies.” What should happen next?

Answer 4 — a supported limitation

“The notes do not establish the allergy policy; obtain the caterer's authoritative policy before answering.” A detailed guarantee would invent evidence. More confident wording cannot repair a missing source.

5. Put these in order: final answer, retrieval observation, model chooses a query, tool searches the notes. Which part runs without an LLM?

Answer 5 — the loop

Model chooses a query → tool searches the notes → retrieval observation → final answer. BM25's local search does not use an LLM; query selection and answer generation do.

Checkpoint: save answers 1–5 in evidence.md and name the evidence you used. For more coding practice, return to Week 3’s RAG practical. Next, you will build a team of agents.

Credit: review adapted from HF Retrieval Agents, Apache-2.0. See Week 3 for the RAG practical.

docs.title: How image observations enter the agent loop
docs.text:
A vision-language model receives pixels as well as text. Passing images=[image] at the start attaches task input. In browser work, the important information may appear only after an action; the agent needs a new screenshot in a later observation before it can reason about the changed page.

Open the full-size original

Original figure, unchanged: HF Vision and Browser Agents. Follow the task image into the task step, then the screenshot into an action step.

Follow the image through the diagram: first as task input, then as an observation after an action. The callback captures the screenshot; the model decides what to do next. In the code you will use, screenshots are attached to ActionStep.observations_images, and the agent’s history is stored in agent.memory.steps.

Before coding: draw one loop for the initial image and a second loop for the browser. Mark where new pixels enter. Predict what would go wrong if the callback saved a PNG file but never attached it to the step. After the browser run, show the action, saved screenshot, and next answer that used it.

Reasoning check

Saving a file is not the same as delivering an image to the model. The screenshot must be included in the observation sent on a later call. Without that new observation the agent may reason from old pixels or guess what changed.

For another example, watch the optional HF browser demonstration. Pause after an action and look for the next screenshot. The exercises below use the venue plan from your download.

docs.title: A. Predict from the image
docs.text:
In File Explorer/Finder, open week04-exercises → assets → venue.png. This image already exists after setup's generator run; do not create an empty file with that name. If it is missing, follow the setup link above.

Under Topic 16 → Image predictions in your existing evidence.md, answer these before calling a model:

1. List three visible facts and one question the image cannot answer.

Image answer 1 — visible facts and a missing fact

Examples: the image labels an ENTRANCE at the upper left, a STAGE at the upper right, and a BUFFET at the lower left. EXIT is labeled at the lower right. It does not establish whether the exit is open now. Choose any three actual visible facts and identify a genuinely missing fact.

2. Is the exit open?

Image answer 2 — exit availability

The picture labels an exit but shows no current closure/open-status information. “There is a labeled exit” is supported; “the exit is open” is not established by these pixels.

3. Does a colored rectangle establish an accessible route?

Image answer 3 — accessibility

No. Colors and room positions do not establish step-free paths, door widths or current access conditions. The model should separate the visible layout from information that needs another source.

Save your predictions. The supplied asset generator uses no LLM; the next program does.

docs.title: B. Build the image agent
docs.text:
Create my_vision.py in your code editor, directly inside week04-exercises, beside week04_common.py. Use New Text File → Save As; it is not supplied. Save with Ctrl + S or Command + S, with a .py extension. If you already have this file, save a copy before replacing its contents.

Add the blocks in B1 → B2 → B3 to this same file, in order. Save it after each part, and run it only after B3.

What this file does — my_vision.py: uses a Groq vision-capable model to inspect the generated venue plan. It has no custom search/browser tools. The answer appears in the terminal, where you compare it with the image you opened.

docs.title: B1. Load the input
docs.text:
Paste this first block to open assets/venue.png as an image.

my_vision.py
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image
from smolagents import CodeAgent
from week04_common import build_model, agent_options, run_task

root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
image = Image.open(root / "assets/venue.png").convert("RGB")
Explain B1 — the image object

root locates your saved script's folder. Pillow reads the existing generated PNG and converts its color mode. This neither creates an agent nor sends pixels to Groq. A filename alone is not the image input.

docs.title: B2. Create the image agent
docs.text:
Add this block below B1. Compare tools=[] with the web specialist’s tool list from Topic 15. What can this agent do without a search tool? Write your answer in evidence.md.

my_vision.py
agent = CodeAgent(
    tools=[],
    model=build_model(),
    **agent_options(max_steps=3),
)
Explain B2 — create the image agent

You create a new CodeAgent object here. tools=[] provides no custom search or browser tools; the built-in final-answer tool is still available. model=build_model() connects the agent to Groq, and max_steps=3 limits its action steps. Image input is attached in the next stage, not by adding a search tool.

docs.title: B3. Give your agent the pixels and a task
docs.text:
Append this last block, then save the same file. Before running, predict one supported label and one unavailable fact.

my_vision.py
run_task(agent,
    "Inspect this fictional venue plan. Name the labeled areas and their relative positions. Separate visible facts from assumptions. Can the image prove whether the exit is currently open? State uncertainty.",
    images=[image],
)
Explain B3 — send pixels, not a path

run_task starts execution. images=[image] attaches actual pixels to this task; a path written in the question would not attach them. Compare the model's answer with your own prediction rather than assuming it interpreted the image correctly.

Build check: which stage creates an agent, which supplies pixels, and why is the search tool absent?

Vision build answer

B2 creates the agent; B3 attaches pixels and starts it. The agent can describe the image you pass in B3 without searching the web. B1 only loads the input. Empty custom tools do not mean there is no LLM.

When: after completing and saving all three blocks B1–B3, your build-check answer and image predictions. Where: in the activated terminal, with its current folder set to week04-exercises.

Run:

python my_vision.py

Enter the Groq key if prompted. Wait for the final result and terminal prompt. What to check: compare each reported label/position with the open image. In the existing evidence.md, paste one supported statement and one uncertain or unsupported statement. This program prints text; it does not generate a new image file.

Try a different question: first copy the original task sentence and its result into your note. In the existing my_vision.py, replace only the complete run_task(...) call at the bottom with the exact block below. Keep the imports, image loading and agent creation above it unchanged. Save the change in the same file.

What this replacement does: the same Groq vision agent receives the same image with a question about a step-free route; its answer is printed in the terminal.

Replace only the run_task call in existing my_vision.py
run_task(agent,
    "Describe a step-free route from ENTRANCE to BUFFET. Separate visible layout from missing accessibility information.",
    images=[image],
)
Explain the change

Only the task text changes. The image is still attached with images=[image], and the same agent/model is used. This lets you compare a new question against the same visible evidence.

When: after copying the first task/result into evidence.md, replacing only the task call above and saving my_vision.py again. Where: the same activated terminal in week04-exercises.

Run again:

python my_vision.py

Wait for the result, then record the changed question and actual answer in your existing evidence.md.

4. Does the image contain enough information for a verified step-free route, and what observation is missing?

Image answer 4 — changed prompt

No. It shows relative areas but no verified ramps, thresholds, widths or passage conditions. Describe the relative positions, then state which accessibility details are missing. The next browser section adds a written access instruction, which is a new observation—not independent physical inspection of a route.

Checkpoint: save both task/result comparisons and your four answers in the existing evidence.md. Keep my_vision.py saved; no second vision program is needed.

docs.title: C. Test a real browser action without an LLM
docs.text:
1. In your code editor, open week04-exercises, with requirements.txt and week04_common.py visible.
  2. Choose File → New Text File → Save As and save my_browser_check.py directly beside them. This file is not in the ZIP; create it now.
  3. Paste the complete code below.
  4. Save with Ctrl + S (Windows) or Command + S (Mac). The name must end in .py, not .py.txt; do not save inside .venv, lessons or assets.

What this file does — my_browser_check.py: Opens the local venue page in a separate Chrome window, clicks its details button, and saves before.png and after.png. It uses Selenium, not an LLM. Open the two screenshots to check the changed observation.

my_browser_check.py
from week04_browser import BrowserSession

browser = BrowserSession()
try:
    print(browser.tools[0]())
    browser.driver.save_screenshot("before.png")
    print(browser.tools[1]())
    browser.driver.save_screenshot("after.png")
    print("Compare before.png and after.png")
finally:
    browser.close()
Explain the code Code What it means BrowserSession() Start a separate Chrome session using the supplied helper. It may obtain a compatible driver. No LLM is used. browser.tools[0]() Call the supplied open_venue tool directly; it opens the generated local HTML file. The first save_screenshot Generate before.png in the current terminal folder. browser.tools[1]() Call show_access_details, which clicks the local page button. The second save_screenshot Generate after.png after the click. finally: browser.close() Close the separate Chrome session even if a later step fails.

The Chrome window may close quickly; inspect the saved PNGs afterwards. This direct test establishes the browser/tool setup before adding a model. Tool success strings are not a substitute for the images.

When: after creating my_browser_check.py, pasting the whole block and saving it; the generated assets/venue.html must already exist. Run this direct check before building/running the browser agent in D. Where: the activated terminal in week04-exercises.

Run:

python my_browser_check.py

The program opens Chrome, performs the click, saves the screenshots and closes Chrome automatically. Wait for the terminal prompt to return. If Chrome or its driver fails, resolve this direct check before the agent run.

What to check: after Chrome closes, open before.png and after.png directly inside week04-exercises in File Explorer/Finder. These are generated screenshots, not files you create or download. If absent, inspect the terminal error. Rerunning this check replaces same-name screenshots.

1. What changed after the click?

Browser answer 1 — changed observation

before.png shows the venue and button without the access paragraph. after.png should show “The east exit is closed for maintenance” and “Use the north entrance for accessible entry.” Read your actual screenshots; if that text is not visible, do not claim the check passed.

2. What does this direct test prove, and what does it not prove?

Browser answer 2 — direct-test scope

It shows that the local page loaded, the supplied click operated and the screenshot changed. It uses no model, so it cannot demonstrate a model choosing the click or receiving/understanding pixels.

In the existing evidence.md, record both screenshot names, the changed text and your two answers. Keep the PNGs in place for review; do not paste HTML source as a substitute for the screenshots.

docs.title: D. Build the browser agent
docs.text:
Create my_browser.py directly in week04-exercises, beside the other scripts. This file is not supplied. Add D1, D2 and D3 to the same file in that order, then save it. If you are replacing an earlier version, save a copy of your work first.

This agent will open the local page, click its details button and use the new screenshot to answer a question. The screenshot callback connects each browser action to the image the model receives next.

What this file does — my_browser.py: uses Groq to choose actions on the local page and receive fresh screenshots after them. Selenium tools operate Chrome; outputs/browser-*.png stores observations. Inspect the terminal trace, image sequence and final answer.

docs.title: D1. Import the parts
docs.text:
my_browser.py
from smolagents import CodeAgent
from week04_common import build_model, agent_options, run_task
from week04_browser import BrowserSession
Explain D1 — tools and screenshots

BrowserSession supplies tools and a screenshot callback. Importing it does not create a model agent. You create the CodeAgent in the next block.

docs.title: D2. Define the browser agent
docs.text:
Add this function below D1. It creates the agent with browser tools and a screenshot callback. You will call the function in D3.

my_browser.py
def build_browser_agent(model, browser):
    return CodeAgent(
        tools=browser.tools,
        model=model,
        step_callbacks=[browser.capture],
        **agent_options(max_steps=6),
    )
Explain D2 — receive screenshots after actions

tools=browser.tools registers opening/clicking actions. step_callbacks=[browser.capture] captures and attaches pixels after each step. The supplied callback writes PNGs to outputs, sets ActionStep.observations_images, records the URL and removes older images from history. Saving a PNG without attaching it would not send it to the model. The callback supplies observations; the agent chooses actions.

docs.title: D3. Open the browser and add the task
docs.text:
Append this final block. Keep the try body indented as shown and finally aligned with try. finally ensures that Chrome closes when the program finishes or an error occurs. Save before running.

my_browser.py
browser = BrowserSession()
try:
    agent = build_browser_agent(build_model(), browser)
    run_task(agent, """Use open_venue first, then inspect its screenshot.
In a separate action step call show_access_details. Inspect the NEW screenshot
before answering: which exit is closed and which entrance is recommended?
Describe the visual evidence and explain what the original venue plan alone
could not establish. Do not combine both tool calls in one action step.
""")
finally:
    browser.close()
Explain D3 — construction, execution and cleanup

The session starts Chrome. Calling build_browser_agent constructs your new agent using that session; run_task starts its decisions. The task requires a later click so the model can compare two states. finally closes Chrome on success or error. Numbered PNGs are generated during execution; browser-*.png is a filename pattern, not a file you create.

Build check: compare this agent with B2. Which two settings connect actions and fresh observations, and what would happen if the callback were absent?

Browser build answer

tools=browser.tools enables actions; step_callbacks=[browser.capture] supplies fresh pixels after them. Without the callback this program would not deliver the new screenshot through its observation loop, so a click-success message alone would not establish what became visible.

When: after C has succeeded, all three blocks D1–D3 are assembled and saved in my_browser.py, and you have answered the build check. Where: the activated terminal in week04-exercises.

Run:

python my_browser.py

Enter the Groq key if prompted. Let the program control its Chrome window and wait for the final result and terminal prompt. What to check: find separate open_venue and show_access_details calls in the terminal, then open the generated numbered PNGs inside week04-exercises/outputs and match the images to the actions. There may be more than two PNGs because the callback also runs after other steps. Use the actual filenames, not an assumed count.

1. Which exit is closed and which entrance is recommended? What supports the answer?

Agent answer 1 — baseline evidence

After the click, the screenshot text says the east exit is closed and recommends the north entrance. The earlier room-label image alone did not establish this. The answer must follow a screenshot returned after the click, not just the tool's “Clicked” message.

2. What if both tools ran in one action step?

Agent answer 2 — separate states

One end-of-step capture may show only the final page. Record that you only received the final state. Check that the task in D3 is copied in full: it asks for the two tools to run in separate steps. To compare before and after, you need a screenshot after each action.

3. What is the callback responsible for?

Agent answer 3 — observation versus decision

The agent/model chooses the action. The callback captures current pixels and attaches them to the step for a later model call. It does not choose the click or guarantee correct interpretation. Initial images=[image] supplies a task image; the callback supplies a new observation after execution.

docs.title: Preserve the baseline and change the practice page
docs.text:
Preserve these generated results before the next run:

  1. Open the existing evidence-files folder from setup. Create a new folder inside it named browser-baseline, using New Folder in your file manager. You create this archive folder manually; it is not generated by Python.
  2. Copy the actual outputs/browser-*.png files into that folder. In the existing evidence.md, paste the baseline action/answer excerpt and list the relevant screenshot names.
  3. In your code editor, open the existing generated assets/venue.html. Do not create a new HTML file or edit a lesson page. Find this exact text in its access-details paragraph:
The east exit is closed for maintenance. Use the north entrance for accessible entry.
  1. Replace only those two sentences with the following fictional test data. Leave the HTML tags and button unchanged:
The west exit is closed for maintenance. Use the south entrance for accessible entry.
  1. Save assets/venue.html. In evidence.md, predict the new answer. Do not rerun prepare_visuals.py, which would restore the original text.
  2. Only after steps 1–5 are complete, return to the same activated terminal in week04-exercises and run python my_browser.py again. The helper starts a new Chrome session and opens your saved local page. Wait for the final result and terminal prompt before step 7. Keep my_browser.py unchanged so you can test whether the answer follows the edited page.
  3. Create browser-revised inside the existing evidence-files folder and copy the new outputs/browser-*.png files there. The callback starts numbering again for each session, so the original outputs may be replaced; use the two archive folders for comparison.

4. Does the new answer follow the changed screenshot?

Agent answer 4 — changed-page comparison

After the saved edit and a fresh run, the newly revealed paragraph should identify the west exit and south entrance. Compare it with the archived east/north baseline. An east/north answer against west/south pixels is unsupported. If it occurs, record it and inspect whether the file was saved, the correct page opened and a fresh screenshot reached the agent.

5. What uncertainty remains even when the answer matches the page?

Agent answer 5 — remaining limit

The screenshot supports what this fictional page says, not an independently verified physical route. It does not establish actual access conditions, and the model can still misread it.

Checkpoint: save the three Python files, your existing evidence.md, direct before.png/after.png, and both archived agent-run screenshot folders. Keep assets/venue.html with your edit, and record the exact two-sentence change. You can restore the original text in that same file after saving the evidence; do not erase the comparison.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and credit
docs.text:
If the generated image/page is missing, run the supplied python prepare_visuals.py in the activated terminal with week04-exercises as its current folder, before returning to A. That replaces existing assets, so first save any page edit you want to preserve in your evidence note. For Chrome errors, confirm Chrome is installed and allow Selenium Manager to obtain its compatible driver; institutional network restrictions may need instructor help. For image-request errors or model limits, check model access and keep only the latest screenshot. A text-only response without an image reaching the model is not a completed vision run.

Problem What to check No such file for a my_*.py program Create that named file using the lesson steps; check its save location and .py extension. Import error for a week04_... helper Check the extracted root and supplied files; use the environment where requirements.txt was installed. Missing before.png / after.png The direct check has not succeeded, or the terminal was in another folder. Inspect its error and current folder. Missing outputs folder No successful report/capture has created it yet. Do not create empty replacement results. Revised run still displays original text Check the saved assets/venue.html, not a second copy, and whether you reran the generator. Compare a fresh screenshot.

docs.title: 1. Choose the kind of agent
docs.text:
HF introduces function-calling agents, which use a model’s structured tool-call interface; ReAct agents, which interpret a text reasoning/action format; and custom agents, which define more specialized behaviour. We use the function-calling route with the classroom model. In AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions, the framework chooses its supported agent route from the model’s metadata.

HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

Read the figure: these are different ways to build the decision loop. Function calling asks the model for a structured tool name and inputs. ReAct uses a text action format that the framework must interpret. Custom agents define their own behavior. A model still needs to follow the chosen format reliably.

Our route: use function calling. For “2 times 2,” the model chooses multiply and supplies a=2, b=2; Python computes 4; the model then answers. Check each part in the printed trace.

An agent can choose the wrong tool or use it with wrong inputs. A final answer alone does not prove that a tool ran. The helper prints REQUEST, actual TOOL calls, their RETURN values and the final ANSWER. Inspect those observations; the lesson does not require exposing a model’s private reasoning.

docs.title: 2. Start with one arithmetic tool
docs.text:
Create my_agent.py. It gives an agent a multiplication function, asks HF’s “2 times 2” question, and prints the tool trace and answer. Groq chooses an action; Python performs the arithmetic. This uses Groq tokens and prints in the terminal.

my_agent.py
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow
from week05_common import get_llm, run, show_agent


def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiply two integers and return the result."""
    return a * b


async def main():
    agent = AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions(
        tools_or_functions=[multiply], llm=get_llm(),
        system_prompt="Use the multiply tool for multiplication. State its returned result.",
        timeout=180,
    )
    await show_agent(agent, "What is 2 times 2? Use the tool.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the agent

The function’s signature/docstring become a tool interface. AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions combines the tools, model and instructions. show_agent starts the workflow and prints completed tool calls. The iteration cap and timeout bound the attempt. The main guard allows other programs to import multiply without running this task.

Run: python my_agent.py.

Find a multiply call with a=2, b=2, a return value of 4, and an answer consistent with it. If no tool call appears, mark the tool-use check incomplete even if the answer is 4. Compare the trace with weather.call(...) in the previous lesson: who selected the operation in each case?

docs.title: 3. Keep memory with Context
docs.text:
Create my_memory.py. It tells the agent “My name is Bob,” asks the name again using the same context, then repeats the question with a fresh context. Inputs are these three messages; the comparison appears in the terminal. All three interactions use Groq tokens.

my_memory.py
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from my_agent import multiply
from week05_common import get_llm, run, show_agent

async def main():
    agent = AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions(
        tools_or_functions=[multiply], llm=get_llm(), timeout=180,
        system_prompt="Answer briefly. Remember only information present in this conversation.",
    )
    ctx = Context(agent)
    await show_agent(agent, "My name is Bob.", ctx=ctx)
    await show_agent(agent, "What was my name again?", ctx=ctx)
    print("NOW A FRESH CONTEXT:")
    await show_agent(agent, "What was my name again?", ctx=Context(agent))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain memory

Context(agent) stores information for the workflow run history. Passing the same ctx connects the first two interactions. The supplied show_agent helper explicitly carries the existing conversation memory into each next run so the earlier messages are retained. A new context does not receive the earlier name. The same model object does not by itself mean the conversation history is shared. This example does not save memory across program restarts.

Predict: which question has the earlier name available? Run: python my_memory.py once.

Check the three answers:

  1. The first acknowledges Bob; the exact greeting may vary.
  2. The same context remembers Bob.
  3. The fresh context says the name is unknown.

If you see UnserializableKeyWarning: the framework cannot serialize its memory object automatically. Our helper carries that object into the next run. Judge this exercise by the answers above. If the second answer forgets Bob, run python week05_common.py and check for version 2026-11-10.2. If yours differs, replace only that helper from the current ZIP and rerun this exercise. Keep your other work.

How the final answer is displayed

Some model replies contain <think> tags or repeat text around </think>. The helper shows the final text after those tags and omits tagged thinking text. This cleans presentation; the tool/source checks still determine whether the answer is supported.

Record the three results in section 22 of evidence.md. A new program run resets the example; keep the supplied Bob messages unchanged.

docs.title: 4. Give the agent a RAG tool
docs.text:
HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

Read the figure: the agent has several possible actions. Document search is one of those actions. It can choose a tool, read its result, then decide how to answer.

In our project: only personas and multiply are available; the picture’s web search and external API are broader examples. A persona question should use personas. A multiplication question should use multiply. Check the selected tool and its return before trusting the final answer.

Create my_rag_agent.py. It gives an agent both multiplication and the persona query tool. The request asks it to search the persona descriptions and return evidence. The query engine and the agent both use Groq; one tool call can therefore involve several model requests. Read the tool trace and final answer in the terminal.

my_rag_agent.py
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow
from my_agent import multiply
from week05_common import get_llm, run, show_agent
from week05_rag import persona_tool

async def main():
    llm = get_llm()
    agent = AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions(
        tools_or_functions=[multiply, persona_tool(llm)], llm=llm, timeout=180,
        system_prompt=("Use personas for questions about profiles and multiply for arithmetic. "
                       "Quote only original EXCERPT text, cite its SOURCE filename, and distinguish it from GENERATED ANSWER text. "
                       "Search results cover only retrieved passages. Say no match was found in those passages; do not claim all profiles were checked. Do not invent names or contact details."),
    )
    await show_agent(agent, "Find the persona interested in Cincinnati art. Use personas and quote its description.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain agentic RAG

A fixed query engine always follows its retrieval-and-answer path. This agent has a choice between tools and can decide what query to send to personas. The returned query-engine answer is an observation for the agent, which may then compose another answer. Inspect both outputs for unsupported additions. return_direct=False allows the agent to use the tool result rather than immediately treating it as the final answer.

Run: python my_rag_agent.py.

Check the result in this order:

  1. Find TOOL: personas and its returned SOURCE and EXCERPT.
  2. Open that source file in data and compare its text with the excerpt.
  3. Check that the final quotation matches the original text and cites the filename.

The separately labeled GENERATED ANSWER is a model summary. If the tool call, original text or citation is missing, record what is incomplete.

Compare tool selection in my_rag_agent.py: find the await show_agent(...) line inside main. Leave the bottom run(main) line alone. Replace the whole request line with this, keeping four leading spaces:

    await show_agent(agent, "What is 2 times 2? Use multiply.")

Save and run python my_rag_agent.py once. Look for TOOL: multiply and RETURN: 4 rather than a persona lookup. Save the trace in evidence.md, then restore and save this exact original line:

    await show_agent(agent, "Find the persona interested in Cincinnati art. Use personas and quote its description.")
Optional: search for a different interest

Optional HF comparison, if capacity allows: save the original request line in evidence.md. In that same place inside main, use this complete line:

    await show_agent(agent, "Search the database for 'science fiction' and return some persona descriptions. Use only the source excerpts. If they contain no match, say no match was found in the retrieved passages; do not claim to have checked every profile.")

Run python my_rag_agent.py once. The tool retrieves at most two passages from ten files. “No match in these passages” is supported if neither mentions science fiction. “No persona in the database likes science fiction” is too broad: the other files were not all checked. Record which claim the answer makes, then restore the original request line shown above.

docs.title: 5. Connect two agents
docs.text:
HF next creates a calculator and an information-lookup agent. Each has its own tools and instructions. An AgentWorkflow has a root agent that receives the user message first. A handoff transfers the active role to another agent; the diagram alone does not prove a handoff took place.

Create my_agent_team.py. It starts with the calculator, then asks for persona research that belongs to info_lookup. This uses the existing index, a shared Groq connection and model tokens. Inspect the terminal for the handoff and the persona search, not just the final answer.

my_agent_team.py
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow, FunctionAgent
from my_agent import multiply
from week05_common import get_llm, run, show_agent
from week05_rag import persona_tool

async def main():
    llm = get_llm()
    calculator = FunctionAgent(
        name="calculator", description="Multiplies integers.",
        system_prompt="Use multiply for math. Hand persona research to info_lookup.",
        tools=[multiply], llm=llm, can_handoff_to=["info_lookup"],
    )
    researcher = FunctionAgent(
        name="info_lookup", description="Searches ten persona descriptions.",
        system_prompt="Use personas. Quote only original EXCERPT text and cite its SOURCE filename. GENERATED ANSWER is not a source quotation. Limit missing-match claims to the retrieved passages. Mark missing information.",
        tools=[persona_tool(llm)], llm=llm, can_handoff_to=["calculator"],
    )
    team = AgentWorkflow(agents=[calculator, researcher], root_agent="calculator", timeout=180)
    await show_agent(team, "Find the Cincinnati art historian. Hand this task to info_lookup, which must query personas.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the team

Two distinct FunctionAgent objects have different names, tools and prompts. can_handoff_to specifies the permitted destinations. root_agent="calculator" selects the entry point. Both receive the same model connection, but remain separate roles. The handoff tool should appear in the trace before personas. The plain arithmetic task from HF can be handled by the calculator alone; this research request deliberately exercises the connection.

Run: python my_agent_team.py. Find the handoff to info_lookup, its personas call, a returned passage and an answer that preserves it. Record the observed handoff and result in section 22.

Checkpoint: save a trace excerpt for arithmetic, the Bob comparison, the RAG tool choice and the handoff. Explain why two agents using one model connection are still two agents.

docs.title: 20 · Build a document question-answer system
docs.text:
Goal: follow the same data through loading, indexing, storing, querying and evaluation. Use the ten persona files created in setup.

HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

Read the figure: start at “Your data” on the left. The index makes that data searchable. A question selects relevant text, which is added to the model request. The model writes an answer from the question and that text.

In our project: “Your data” is ten persona files. Asking about Cincinnati should retrieve persona_0.txt. Retrieval finds the passage; Groq writes the answer. You still compare the answer with the original passage, because a generated answer can contain mistakes.

docs.title: 1. Understand the five stages
docs.text:
Stage What happens What to inspect Loading Read text files into Document objects. File names and document count. Indexing Split documents into Node chunks and embed their text. Chunk count and settings. Storing Save vectors and metadata in Chroma. The generated alfred_chroma_db folder. Querying Retrieve similar chunks, then optionally generate an answer. Retrieved text, source names and answer. Evaluation Check whether the answer is supported and useful. Source comparison and any evaluator feedback.

A Node is a chunk linked to its source document. Store the vectors rather than re-embedding every time you ask a question. Use the same embedding model for documents and questions so their vectors can be compared.

docs.title: 2. Load, split, embed and store
docs.text:
Create my_ingest.py. It reads the ten local text files, splits them, computes embeddings on your CPU and saves them in a Chroma database. It uses no generative LLM and no Groq tokens. The first embedding run needs internet to download the model; counts and the saved folder are visible in the terminal/file manager.

my_ingest.py
from llama_index.core import SimpleDirectoryReader
from llama_index.core.ingestion import IngestionPipeline
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter
from week05_common import ROOT, run
from week05_rag import embedding_model, get_store

async def main():
    files = [ROOT / "data" / f"persona_{number}.txt" for number in range(10)]
    missing = [path.name for path in files if not path.is_file()]
    if missing:
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            "Missing persona files: " + ", ".join(missing)
            + ". Run python prepare_personas.py; see setup troubleshooting if data is incomplete."
        )
    documents = SimpleDirectoryReader(
        input_files=[str(path) for path in files], filename_as_id=True,
    ).load_data()
    print("Documents:", len(documents))
    if len(documents) != 10:
        raise ValueError("Use the ten supplied-dataset persona files for this first run.")
    collection, vector_store = get_store()
    if collection.count():
        if collection.count() < len(documents):
            raise ValueError("The saved index is incomplete. Close its programs, rename alfred_chroma_db as a backup, then rerun my_ingest.py.")
        print("Index already exists. Reuse it; no documents were added.")
        return
    pipeline = IngestionPipeline(
        transformations=[
            SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=256, chunk_overlap=20),
            embedding_model(),
        ],
        vector_store=vector_store,
    )
    nodes = await pipeline.arun(documents=documents)
    print("Indexed chunks:", len(nodes))
    print("Stored vectors:", collection.count())
    print("Saved in alfred_chroma_db/")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the pipeline

files names the ten intended persona files explicitly. A missing file produces a message telling you what to download. SimpleDirectoryReader reads that list and preserves each filename as metadata, including when an ancestor folder is hidden. SentenceSplitter uses a 256-token target with a 20-token overlap; the documents are short, so a document may fit in one chunk. The embedding transformation uses BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5. get_store() returns a local Chroma collection named alfred and its LlamaIndex adapter. pipeline.arun performs the transformations and stores the nodes. An existing non-empty collection is reused, preventing duplicate ingestion on a simple rerun.

Save and run: python my_ingest.py.

Check Documents: 10, a positive chunk/vector count, and alfred_chroma_db beside your script. Do not expect a model answer yet. Run the same file again: it should say the index already exists. The stored count should not grow.

If you later change the data or embedding settings, the old database does not update automatically. Preserve your evidence, close all programs using it, rename the generated alfred_chroma_db folder as a backup, and rerun ingestion to create a fresh database. Keep the original ten-file dataset unchanged for the first exercise. If indexing was interrupted, use this same fresh-database procedure rather than trusting a partial index.

docs.title: 3. Test retrieval before generation
docs.text:
Create my_retrieve.py. It opens your stored index, embeds one question locally and prints the two most similar chunks with filenames and similarity scores. It uses no Groq model or tokens. After the embedding files are cached, this check can run without a model service.

my_retrieve.py
from week05_rag import open_index

index = open_index()
retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=2)
hits = retriever.retrieve("Cincinnati art historian and museum professional")
for hit in hits:
    print("FILE:", hit.node.metadata.get("file_name"))
    print("SCORE:", round(hit.score or 0.0, 3))
    print("TEXT:", hit.node.get_content())
    print()
Explain retrieval

open_index() reopens the database using the same embedding model. It refuses to proceed if no vectors are stored. as_retriever returns chunks and scores, not a generated answer. The top-two setting is a result count, not proof that both chunks are relevant. A similarity score is not a probability that a claim is true.

Run: python my_retrieve.py.

Look for persona_0.txt and the description of a Cincinnati art historian. Open that file and compare its text with the output. Save the source name and relevant passage in section 20 of your evidence note.

Try a comparison in the same my_retrieve.py: find this complete line:

hits = retriever.retrieve("Cincinnati art historian and museum professional")

Replace that line with this one, save, and run python my_retrieve.py:

hits = retriever.retrieve("What is this person's full legal name?")

The retriever may still return two chunks. Does either contain the name? Record why returning text is different from answering the question. Then restore the first line, save, and keep the original Cincinnati version for later review. Do not replace the whole file or change its imports.

Retrieval check

The dataset contains descriptions, not named people. Similarity search still returns candidates for an unsupported question. Inspect their contents and mark the requested name missing.

docs.title: 4. Add a query engine and inspect its answer
docs.text:
Create my_query.py. It uses the stored index and Groq to answer one question about the descriptions. It prints both the generated answer and the retrieved source passages. This program uses Groq tokens; its output is in the terminal.

my_query.py
from week05_common import get_llm, run
from week05_rag import open_index

async def main():
    engine = open_index().as_query_engine(
        llm=get_llm(), similarity_top_k=2,
        response_mode="tree_summarize", use_async=True,
    )
    question = "Which persona is interested in Cincinnati's cultural heritage? Use only the supplied descriptions; do not invent a name."
    response = await engine.aquery(question)
    print("QUESTION:", question)
    print("ANSWER:", response)
    for source in response.source_nodes:
        print("SOURCE:", source.node.metadata.get("file_name"))
        print(source.node.get_content())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the query engine

as_query_engine combines retrieval with answer generation. tree_summarize combines retrieved content through a summarization strategy and can require multiple model calls. use_async=True allows async response synthesis, and aquery awaits the result in this ordinary script. source_nodes lets you inspect the passages used. It does not prove the answer is faithful: you must compare it with those passages.

Run: python my_query.py.

Check that the answer describes the art historian and does not invent a name. Match each factual detail to the printed source. Record any unsupported statement as an error even if the program ran successfully.

More about query interfaces and response strategies

HF distinguishes three interfaces: retriever returns passages; query engine produces a response for a question; chat engine supports conversational interaction. We use the query engine here. Its response strategies include refine (work through chunks successively), compact (pack context to reduce calls) and tree_summarize (combine summaries). They organize model calls; none guarantees correctness.

Optional: ask about writing or travel

Optional comparison — change the topic: look for a profile with an interest in writing or travel. This asks you to find and describe an existing profile.

In my_query.py, copy the current question = ... line into evidence.md so you can restore it. Replace that line inside main with this, keeping four leading spaces:

    question = "Find a persona interested in writing or travel. Describe it using only the supplied text. If the retrieved passages contain no matching interest, say no match was found in those passages."

Save and run python my_query.py once if capacity allows. Compare the answer with the printed sources: does a source actually mention writing or travel? If not, record “No match in the retrieved passages.” Two returned passages cannot establish that none of the ten profiles matches.

After recording your finding, restore this exact original line inside main, keeping four leading spaces, and save:

    question = "Which persona is interested in Cincinnati's cultural heritage? Use only the supplied descriptions; do not invent a name."

docs.title: 5. Evaluate and observe
docs.text:
First do a manual check: does each detail in the answer appear in the retrieved text? This needs no additional model call. Faithfulness asks whether the answer is supported by context. Relevance asks whether it addresses the question. Correctness asks whether it matches a trusted answer or facts. These are different checks.

Optional model check — create my_evaluate.py. It generates a short answer, then asks an LLM-based evaluator to judge support against the retrieved text. It prints the answer, judgement, feedback and sources. Both generation and evaluation use Groq tokens; run only after the earlier source check works.

my_evaluate.py
from llama_index.core.evaluation import FaithfulnessEvaluator
from week05_common import get_llm, run
from week05_rag import open_index

async def main():
    llm = get_llm()
    engine = open_index().as_query_engine(
        llm=llm, similarity_top_k=2, response_mode="compact", use_async=True,
    )
    response = await engine.aquery("Describe the Cincinnati art historian using only the provided text.")
    print("ANSWER:", response)
    judgement = await FaithfulnessEvaluator(llm=llm).aevaluate_response(response=response)
    print("PASS:", judgement.passing)
    print("FEEDBACK:", judgement.feedback)
    for source in response.source_nodes:
        print("SOURCE:", source.node.metadata.get("file_name"))
        print(source.node.get_content())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the evaluation

FaithfulnessEvaluator judges whether the response is supported by its retrieved context. It is another model-based judgement, so it can be wrong. passing=True is evidence about that check, not a certificate of factual correctness. Compare its feedback with the actual passages. This test does not establish facts outside the dataset.

Optional run: python my_evaluate.py. Save your comparison of manual and model judgements. Mark “not attempted” if you skip this additional model call.

HF also introduces observability: recording what the components did. Your printed source names, passages, counts and later tool trace provide local evidence. HF’s Phoenix/LlamaTrace integration adds an external tracing service and an additional account/key; it is an optional extension, not needed for this local exercise. Do not paste credentials into tracing examples.

docs.title: 18 · Introduction to LlamaIndex
docs.text:
Goal: explain the four parts you will connect this week. Complete setup first.

Alfred needs to answer questions about a collection of persona descriptions. A model may know many general facts, but it has not automatically read these local files. You will give Alfred a way to search them and use the returned information.

HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

The idea in one example: ask, “Which persona is interested in Cincinnati art?” LlamaIndex helps your program find the relevant text and give it to the model. You will first build that search, then let an agent choose when to use it. Finally, you will connect operations through workflow steps.

docs.title: Four parts, four jobs
docs.text:
Part Its job This week’s example Component Perform one part of an application. Load files, create embeddings, retrieve passages or generate an answer. Tool Expose a capability with a name, description and inputs. Multiply numbers or search the persona collection. Agent Let a model choose tools and use their results. Decide between arithmetic and persona lookup. Workflow Connect steps through typed events and shared state. Pass a result to the next step, loop once or hand off to another agent.

An embedding is a list of numbers representing text for similarity search. An index organizes the stored information so it can be searched. A query engine retrieves relevant passages and uses a model to compose an answer. Retrieval supplies evidence; it does not guarantee that the answer is correct.

docs.title: Follow the information
docs.text:
Persona files → text chunks → embeddings → stored index
Question → retrieve relevant chunks → model composes answer
Agent → chooses a tool → receives its result → answers or takes another step
Workflow → event → matching step → another event or a final result

These ideas connect to your earlier RAG and tool exercises. Here you will build them with LlamaIndex and inspect each boundary: which part retrieves, which part calls a model, and which part decides what happens next.

LlamaIndex’s workflow system is event driven: the kind of event determines which step can run. It is async first: await waits for an operation’s result without blocking other async work. You do not need to write parallel programs to use it. Each lesson supplies a normal script entry point so you can run python filename.py.

docs.title: Check your understanding
docs.text:

Answer

No. A fixed retrieval-and-answer pipeline can run without an agent deciding which tool to use. Find the decision loop and actual tool calls before calling it an agent.
