docs.title: Week 05 · LlamaIndex
docs.text:
Goal: build an assistant that searches your documents, uses tools, and passes work through clear steps.

Complete Week 4 first. This week follows HF Unit 2.2 in the same order. Keep your earlier work. Use a new week05-exercises folder, Python 3.11, your editor and terminal. No notebook or GPU is required. English and Japanese use the same code and exercises.

docs.title: Follow this route
docs.text:
Order Lesson What you will do Setup This page Install a separate environment and download ten persona descriptions. 18 Introduction Distinguish components, tools, agents and workflows. 19 LlamaHub Match an integration package to its Python import; test the model connection. 20 Components Load, split, embed, store, retrieve and query the persona data; inspect evidence. 21 Tools Make a function tool, a query-engine tool and a local tool collection. Check Quiz 1 Explain components and tools before creating an agent. 22 Agents Use arithmetic tools, remember Bob, search personas and hand off a task. 23 Workflows Connect events and steps, make a bounded loop, draw the flow and share state. Check Quiz 2 Explain agent decisions, events, memory and shared state. Review Conclusion and completion Show your working files and explain the results.

The persona search, demo weather, arithmetic, Bob memory and workflow examples follow the HF unit. You will run them as saved Python programs. We keep the classroom Groq connection; no new model-provider account is needed.

docs.title: 1. Download and open the new folder
docs.text:
Download the Week 5 English/Japanese starter

  1. Save the ZIP. On Windows, right-click it and choose Extract All. On Mac, double-click it in Finder.
  2. Open the extracted folder and find the folder containing requirements.txt and week05_common.py. On Mac, this is usually the extracted week05-exercises folder itself. Windows may add an extra outer folder. Move the folder containing those files into agent-course, beside your earlier exercise folders. Name it week05-exercises.
  3. Open week05-exercises with VS Code → File → Open Folder. You should see requirements.txt, prepare_personas.py, week05_common.py and week05_rag.py together.
  4. Keep these supplied helpers. The my_*.py files are not in the ZIP: you will create them from the lessons, beside the helpers. Read the online lessons or the Markdown copies in lessons/en and lessons/ja.
Supplied file Purpose requirements.txt Tested Week 5 packages, separate from smolagents. prepare_personas.py Downloads ten public persona descriptions without an LLM. week05_common.py Loads local settings, connects to Groq and prints tool-call results. week05_rag.py Reopens the local index for later lessons, avoiding repeated setup code. README.md, NOTICE.md, HF-LICENSE.txt Setup summary, sources and license. lessons/en, lessons/ja Matching English and Japanese lesson sequences. images/huggingface-week05 Original HF figures used by the lesson copies. Click a figure to open it at full size.

docs.title: 2. Create and activate a separate environment
docs.text: Use 64-bit Python 3.11 on a supported Windows or Mac system. Check that your computer has room for the packages and model files before installing. In the Mac walkthrough, the environment alone used about 1.6 GB; usage varies by computer. Installation includes local embedding libraries and can download large packages. Internet is required for installation, the persona download, the first embedding-model download and Groq requests. Later retrieval and plain workflows run locally. Keep the terminal open after activation.

docs.title: Choose the terminal and check Python
docs.text:
Windows in VS Code: open Terminal → New Terminal. If its prompt begins with PS, it is PowerShell. Click the arrow beside the terminal’s + button and choose Command Prompt. For future terminals, use Ctrl + Shift + P → Terminal: Select Default Profile → Command Prompt, then open a new terminal. The commands below use Command Prompt. See VS Code terminal profiles.

Check Python before creating the environment:

  • Windows Command Prompt: run py -3.11 --version.
  • Mac Terminal: run python3.11 --version.

Continue when the result is Python 3.11.x. If the command is missing or cannot find 3.11, open the instructions below first.

Python 3.11 is missing

Windows 10/11: install the Python install manager from python.org. Close and reopen VS Code so its terminal sees the installation. In a new Command Prompt, run these lines:

pymanager install 3.11
py -3.11 --version

pymanager avoids a conflict with an older py launcher. If either command is still missing, follow Python’s Windows troubleshooting, or ask your instructor for help with the command and error shown.

Mac: if Homebrew is installed, run:

brew install python@3.11
python3.11 --version

If brew is missing, install it using the instructions at brew.sh, including the installer’s Next steps for your terminal, then run the two lines above. Homebrew’s Python 3.11 page lists supported systems. For a managed or unsupported computer, ask your instructor before continuing.

docs.title: Install the Week 5 packages
docs.text:
Windows — Command Prompt, one line at a time:

cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\agent-course\week05-exercises"
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat
python --version
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip check
python week05_common.py
python prepare_personas.py

Mac — Terminal, one line at a time:

cd ~/agent-course/week05-exercises
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python --version
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip check
python week05_common.py
python prepare_personas.py

Use your actual folder path if it differs. Check for (.venv), Python 3.11.x, No broken requirements found., Week 5 starter version: 2026-11-10.2, and Saved 10 persona files in data/ (no LLM, no Groq tokens). The version check prints only the helper version; it makes no model request. The download also creates dataset-source.json. Open data/persona_0.txt; it should describe a Cincinnati art historian. These are profile descriptions, not identified real people. Some source descriptions may be incomplete; do not repair them by guessing.

prepare_personas.py obtains the first ten records from the same HF persona dataset used in HF’s notebook. If the rows service fails or truncates text, it downloads the original dataset file (about 35 MB), verifies it, and reads the same ten complete descriptions. Only those texts are saved; no HF token is needed. It will not overwrite a non-empty data folder. Wait for the saved-file message. If downloading stops, follow its printed diagnosis before continuing. First embedding use downloads BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 into .cache/huggingface inside this folder. Later runs load the complete cache locally without checking HF. It runs on your CPU and does not use Groq tokens.

In a new terminal, repeat only the folder-change and activation lines. Do not recreate the environment every lesson.

docs.title: 3. Create your local settings
docs.text:
Reusing Week 4’s key: copy only the GROQ_API_KEY value into this new file. If you copied the whole .env, replace its GROQ_MODEL line with the exact line below. Week 4 used a provider prefix such as groq/; this week uses the plain Groq model ID. Keep your Week 4 file as it is.

In the editor, create .env directly in week05-exercises, beside week05_common.py. Save it as .env, not .env.txt. Paste this and replace the key placeholder:

GROQ_API_KEY=your_own_groq_api_key
GROQ_MODEL=qwen/qwen3.8-27b

The helper explicitly calls load_dotenv before reading the settings. Creating the file alone does not make Python read it. Existing terminal environment values take priority. If you previously set GROQ_MODEL in this terminal, clear it with set GROQ_MODEL= in Windows Command Prompt or unset GROQ_MODEL on Mac, then rerun. Keep the key on your computer; do not include .env in GitHub, screenshots or your evidence.

The model is listed on Groq’s model page, checked 2026-11-09. It is a preview model; check current availability and your permissions if a run fails. Use the plain model ID shown above. The current helper also removes a leading groq/ from a copied value, but it cannot update an old model name for you. The programs send prompts and retrieved persona passages to Groq. Use the public sample data for these exercises.

Run model programs one at a time. Each agent run has a six-iteration cap and no automatic API retries. A query tool can make several model requests. If Groq returns 429, stop and check account limits, credits and the retry interval. Waiting can reset a short rate window; it does not add credits or guarantee success.

docs.title: 4. Start an evidence note
docs.text:
Create evidence.md in the same folder. Paste these headings, then save. Add short actual output and your own explanations after each lesson. This note is not a Python program.

evidence.md

## 19 — Integration and model connection
## 20 — Ingestion, retrieval, answer, sources, evaluation
## 21 — Function tool, query tool, ToolSpec and utility tools

## 22 — Tool calls, Bob memory, RAG and handoff
## 23 — Events, loop, flow diagram and shared counter

For every later file: File → New Text File → Save As, save the exact .py name beside the helpers, paste the blocks in order and save with Ctrl + S or Command + S. Do not put your programs inside .venv or lessons.

Work on one program at a time. Do not create all the files in advance. Each lesson ends with a short file/result checklist. Keep earlier programs because later examples import them. There are 17 required small programs and one optional evaluator across the whole week; you do not need to understand or build them all at setup.

Setup checkpoint: your folder should contain the supplied helpers, .venv, .env, evidence.md, dataset-source.json, and data/persona_0.txt through data/persona_9.txt. No my_*.py file is required yet. The first one is created in the LlamaHub lesson.

docs.title: If a step stops
docs.text:
Find the error and its next action What you see Next action python: can't open file Check that the terminal is in week05-exercises, that you saved the named file beside the helpers, and that its name is not .py.txt. Wrong or missing starter version Replace only week05_common.py with the copy from the current Week 5 ZIP. Keep your .env, data and student programs. Rerun python week05_common.py. ModuleNotFoundError Activate this week’s .venv using the instructions above, then rerun python -m pip install -r requirements.txt. Do not install into Week 4. Dataset download stops HTTP 503 means a server failure: try later. For a connection timeout, check the network and retry. A checksum failure means the original file was incomplete or changed. No persona files are written on these failures; keep the message for your instructor. Missing persona_*.txt Run python prepare_personas.py. If data is incomplete and the downloader refuses to overwrite it, preserve it by renaming it data-backup, then rerun the download. The embedding model cannot finish loading Check internet access and free disk space, then rerun the same program. The public download can resume; a failed download does not mean the model is private. If it keeps failing, close the programs, rename .cache/huggingface to .cache/huggingface-backup, and retry when the connection is stable. Keep your data and source files. This download does not use Groq tokens. The index is missing or incomplete Finish the ten-file download, then run python my_ingest.py. If a partial database exists, close its programs, rename alfred_chroma_db as a backup, and run ingestion again. Groq 401 Check the key in your local .env; do not print it or send it in evidence. Groq 403/404 Check the Week 5 model ID and your account’s model permissions. If you copied Week 4 settings, replace the model line using step 3. Groq 413 Keep the small dataset and short task; waiting does not shrink an oversized request. Groq 429 Stop and follow the model-limit guidance in step 3. flow.html is blank Follow the drawing check in lesson 23. The current helper embeds the graph libraries; internet is not required to view the saved diagram.

Fix the current checkpoint before continuing to a program that depends on it. If you need help, record the filename, command and error category without including .env or your key.

docs.title: 19 · Find and use integrations
docs.text:
Goal: identify the packages that connect your program to a model, embeddings and storage. Use the activated terminal from setup.

HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

Read the figure: LlamaHub is a catalog of ready-made connections. The categories help you find a model connection, a document reader, a database adapter or a tool. You choose the parts your program needs; you do not install the whole catalog.

In our project: the Groq integration sends requests to the model, the Hugging Face integration creates local embeddings, and the Chroma integration stores searchable text. The table below connects each package name to its Python import.

docs.title: 1. What LlamaHub provides
docs.text:
LlamaHub is a catalog of integrations. Find a component by the job you need it to do. A package installs the code; a Python import loads that code into your program. The names are related but not identical.

Job Package in your requirements Import used in this week Core components and tools llama-index-core llama_index.core Classroom Groq model llama-index-llms-groq llama_index.llms.groq Local Hugging Face embeddings llama-index-embeddings-huggingface llama_index.embeddings.huggingface Chroma vector storage llama-index-vector-stores-chroma llama_index.vector_stores.chroma Workflow drawing llama-index-utils-workflow llama_index.utils.workflow

You already installed these together in setup. Do not install a second set of packages into your Week 4 environment. A working integration also needs its runtime inputs: the Groq connection needs a key and model ID; local embeddings need model files; storage needs a local directory.

docs.title: 2. Test one model request
docs.text:
Create my_llm.py in week05-exercises. This program reads your local settings, sends the greeting below to Groq, and prints the response in the terminal. It uses an LLM and Groq tokens. It does not index or search any documents.

my_llm.py
from week05_common import get_llm, run

async def main():
    llm = get_llm()
    response = await llm.acomplete("Hello, how are you?")
    print(response.text)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the code

get_llm() loads .env and returns the configured Groq integration. acomplete is the async completion method; await waits for its response. run(main) calls asyncio.run(main()) in the supplied helper, so a normal terminal can execute it. The main guard prevents a model request when another file imports this module.

Save and run: python my_llm.py.

A short greeting is enough to verify the connection. Wording varies. If it fails, check .env, the active environment, network access and model permissions. Do not print the API key. The helper labels a failed run incomplete; save the error category in section 19 of your evidence note.

Check: did this program use your persona files? Which line actually requested a model response?

Answer

It did not read persona files. The request happens at await llm.acomplete(...); constructing the integration alone does not request a completion.

Source and adapted examples: HF Unit 2.2 — llama-hub. Apache-2.0; see the starter’s NOTICE.md and HF-LICENSE.txt.

docs.title: Stop and check
docs.text:
New file to keep Result to confirm my_llm.py A short model greeting appears without an error.

Do not change this file for the next lesson. If the greeting failed, use setup troubleshooting before the model-dependent exercises. Record the successful greeting or the actual failure in section 19 of your note.

Next: 20 · Components and RAG.

docs.title: Week 5 · Quiz 1
docs.text: Goal: explain components and tools before you use them in an agent. Write your answers under Quiz 1 in evidence.md, then open the explanations. These are classroom self-checks following the topics of HF Quiz 1; they do not submit a score to HF.

docs.title: 1. Query engine
docs.text:
How does a query engine differ from the retriever you ran?

Answer 1

The retriever returns candidate passages and scores. A query engine also uses a model to compose an answer from retrieved information. Both need their outputs checked.

docs.title: 2. Function tool
docs.text:
What does FunctionTool add to a Python function? Does calling it directly require an LLM?

Answer 2

It exposes the function through a tool interface with a name, description and input schema. A direct call runs the function without an LLM deciding to use it.

docs.title: 3. Tool collection
docs.text:
Your ClassroomToolSpec returns two tools. How many agents did it create?

Answer 3

Zero. It groups capabilities into a list. An agent is created separately and can be given that list.

docs.title: 4. Clear interface
docs.text:
Why is “search ten persona descriptions for interests and expertise” a better description than “a useful tool”? Which parts of a function help form its schema?

Answer 4

The specific description helps a model decide when the tool is appropriate and what information it can supply. The function’s name, parameter names, type annotations and docstring describe its inputs and purpose. Metadata can be inferred, but should be inspected and clarified.

Ready to continue: locate one actual source passage and explain which tool could retrieve it. If you cannot, revisit components and tools.

Next: 22 · Agents.

docs.title: Week 5 · Quiz 2
docs.text: Goal: explain how agent decisions, events and state work together. Answer under Quiz 2 in evidence.md before opening the explanations. These classroom checks follow the topics of HF Quiz 2; they do not submit a score.

docs.title: 1. AgentWorkflow
docs.text:
What does AgentWorkflow organize? Does constructing it prove that its agents handed off a task?

Answer 1

It organizes one or more agents and their tools, including permitted handoffs. Construction shows configuration. An actual tool/handoff trace shows execution.

docs.title: 2. Shared state
docs.text:
Which object held the stored query and the team’s arithmetic counter? How is it different from ProcessingEvent?

Answer 2

Context held shared state. ProcessingEvent carried a typed payload between matching steps and determined routing. Both can carry information, but their roles in the workflow differ.

docs.title: 3. Conversation memory
docs.text:
Why did both Bob messages use the same ctx? Would a new context automatically know his name?

Answer 3

Passing the same context retains the earlier interaction. A new context has no evidence of that earlier name. Guessing the name is not remembering it.

docs.title: 4. Agentic RAG
docs.text:
How does an agent with arithmetic and persona tools differ from calling the persona query engine directly?

Answer 4

The direct query follows a fixed retrieval-and-answer operation. The agent can choose between available tools and formulate their inputs. You must inspect which tool it actually chose and whether the returned evidence supports the final answer.

Extra check: ARITHMETIC CALLS: 1 appears in your output. Does that mean there was only one Groq request?

Counter answer

No. The counter counts only executions of the arithmetic functions. Handoffs and decisions can require other model requests. It is not a request or token meter.

Next: Conclusion and completion.

docs.title: 21 · Give components a tool interface
docs.text:
Goal: make your existing functions and document query engine available through clear tool interfaces. Finish the components lesson first.

HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

Read the figure: each card shows a way to make a capability available to an agent. A FunctionTool exposes a Python function. A QueryEngineTool exposes document search and answering. A ToolSpec groups related tools. Utility tools help load or search a large tool result. The figure calls the second card “Search Engine”; our code uses QueryEngineTool.

In our project: first call the demo weather function yourself. Then call the persona query tool yourself. Later, an agent will choose which tool to call. A tool has a name, inputs and a result; creating one does not create an agent.

docs.title: 1. FunctionTool: expose a Python function
docs.text:
Create my_tools.py. Following HF’s weather example, it returns a fixed “sunny” string and prints the tool’s name, description and input schema. This is demo data, not live weather. It uses no LLM or Groq tokens. Read its terminal output before allowing an agent to use it.

my_tools.py
from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool


def get_weather(location: str) -> str:
    """Return a fixed classroom weather example, not live weather."""
    print(f"Getting demo weather for {location}")
    return f"The weather in {location} is sunny (demo data)"


weather = FunctionTool.from_defaults(
    get_weather, name="my_weather_tool",
    description="Return fixed demo weather for a location. Not a live forecast.",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(weather.call("New York"))
    print("NAME:", weather.metadata.name)
    print("DESCRIPTION:", weather.metadata.description)
    print("INPUT SCHEMA:", weather.metadata.fn_schema.model_json_schema())
Explain the function tool

FunctionTool.from_defaults wraps a Python function. Type annotations describe its inputs; its name and description tell a model what it can do. weather.call directly runs the function. The main guard means importing get_weather later will not execute these checks. A tool can run without an agent.

Run: python my_tools.py.

Look for the New York demo message, tool name and a schema containing a string input called location. Inside the main guard of this same file, replace only this line:

    print(weather.call("New York"))

with:

    print(weather.call("Tokyo"))

Keep four leading spaces. Save and run python my_tools.py again. Why does the answer remain sunny? After recording the result, restore the New York line and save. Do not change get_weather or the tool definition.

Answer

The function always returns the same pattern. It does not contact a weather service. A realistic-looking sentence is not evidence of a live lookup.

docs.title: 2. QueryEngineTool: expose your document search
docs.text:
Create my_query_tool.py. It wraps the same persona query engine in a named tool, calls that tool directly and prints its result. It uses Groq to compose an answer, but no agent chooses the tool yet. Its inputs are the stored persona index and the question below.

my_query_tool.py
from week05_common import get_llm, run
from week05_rag import persona_tool

async def main():
    tool = persona_tool(get_llm())
    print("TOOL:", tool.metadata.name, tool.metadata.description)
    result = await tool.acall("Describe the persona interested in Cincinnati art. Do not invent a real name.")
    print("RETURN:", result)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the query tool

Open week05_rag.py and find persona_tool. It creates an evidence-preserving QueryEngineTool with the query engine, name personas, a specific description and return_direct=False. The description explains the dataset and its limits. The compact query engine uses at most two retrieved chunks. acall calls this tool asynchronously. The supplied evidence-preserving QueryEngineTool also attaches the response’s original source nodes, labeled SOURCE and EXCERPT, before the separate GENERATED ANSWER. That lets you and the agent distinguish original wording from generated prose. Returning the result to an agent later can lead to another model call to compose the final answer.

Run: python my_query_tool.py. Compare its result with my_query.py. Find SOURCE: persona_0.txt, then compare its EXCERPT with that file in data. Treat text labeled GENERATED ANSWER as generated prose, not a quotation. If a source excerpt is clipped, open the file for the rest. Do not count a direct tool call as an agent’s decision.

docs.title: 3. ToolSpec: collect related tools
docs.text:
HF demonstrates a community GmailToolSpec. Connecting Gmail requires its own setup and account permissions. First learn the same collection mechanism with the local weather/arithmetic tools below. This exercise does not connect to an email account.

Create my_toolspec.py. It groups two Python functions into a tool list and prints each name/description before calling both directly. It uses no LLM, network or Groq tokens.

my_toolspec.py
from llama_index.core.tools.tool_spec.base import BaseToolSpec
from my_tools import get_weather

class ClassroomToolSpec(BaseToolSpec):
    spec_functions = ["weather", "multiply"]

    def weather(self, location: str) -> str:
        """Return fixed classroom weather, not a live forecast."""
        return get_weather(location)

    def multiply(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        """Multiply two integers."""
        return a * b

tools = ClassroomToolSpec().to_tool_list()
for tool in tools:
    print(tool.metadata.name, "=>", tool.metadata.description)
print(tools[0].call("New York"))
print(tools[1].call(a=2, b=2))
Explain the tool collection

spec_functions names the methods to expose. to_tool_list() creates individual tools from them. A ToolSpec is a collection, not an agent. The list can be inspected before it is given to an agent. The method docstrings describe each tool’s purpose.

Run: python my_toolspec.py. Expect two tool descriptions, demo weather and 4. Write down why adding tools does not add agents.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text: HF next introduces an MCP ToolSpec. MCP is a protocol for exposing tools from a separate server. The server must exist and be running; installing a client does not create one. The result is still a list of callable tools. This is a reading extension here: no external server or personal account is required to complete the week. See HF’s tools lesson for its Gmail and MCP integration examples.

docs.title: 4. Utility tools: avoid handing over huge results
docs.text:
A tool can return more text than an agent needs. HF describes two useful patterns:

Pattern What it does On-demand loader Load data, index it and answer a query when the tool is called. Load-and-search tool collection One tool loads/indexes a large result; another searches that stored result for the requested information.

Both patterns let an agent work with a focused answer rather than repeatedly receiving an entire large response. They may add embedding work, storage and model calls. They do not automatically prove the returned information is correct. Your small persona query tool already demonstrates why retrieved excerpts are easier to inspect than a whole collection.

Check: a service returns 100 long records but the user asks about only one. What would a load-and-search tool collection change, and what still needs checking?

Answer

It would index the large result and let the agent search for the relevant part. You would still check whether the selected record supports the answer, whether anything important was omitted, and what model calls or storage were used.

Checkpoint: in section 21 of your evidence note, identify a direct function call, a direct query-tool call and a tool collection. None of these alone demonstrates agent tool selection.

Source and adapted examples: HF Unit 2.2 — tools. Apache-2.0; see the starter’s NOTICE.md and HF-LICENSE.txt.

docs.title: Stop and check
docs.text:
New file to keep Result to confirm my_tools.py Demo weather, a name/description, and a location input schema. Restore New York after the comparison. my_query_tool.py A tool return with original SOURCE/EXCERPT text separate from GENERATED ANSWER. my_toolspec.py Two tool descriptions and their direct-call results.

Keep earlier components files and these three new files. Do not edit supplied helpers. Explain in section 21 of your note why a tool collection is not an agent.

Next: Quiz 1.

docs.title: 23 · Connect steps with events
docs.text:
Goal: control how information moves between steps, then connect that control to an agent team. Follow these sections in order, as in HF. All programs are separate files beside your existing helpers.

HF original figure, unchanged. Source lesson · Enlarge the figure.

Read the figure: blue boxes are steps that do work. Colored ovals are events: messages that carry data and make the next matching step eligible to run. Follow a path such as StartEvent → parse_query → QueryEvent → run_query → StopEvent. The picture shows a larger workflow; you will start with one step.

A simple way to picture it: a step does a job, then passes a labeled message. The label tells the workflow which step can receive it. The message carries the result that the next step needs. You write those connections using event types such as ProcessingEvent.

docs.title: 1. A one-step workflow
docs.text:
A workflow starts with a StartEvent. A matching step receives it and returns another event. A StopEvent ends the run and carries its result. @step registers a method; type annotations tell the workflow which events it accepts and emits.

Create my_workflow.py. It runs one step and prints “Hello, world!” in the terminal. It uses no LLM, network or Groq tokens. The only input is the workflow’s start event.

my_workflow.py
from llama_index.core.workflow import StartEvent, StopEvent, Workflow, step
from week05_common import run

class MyWorkflow(Workflow):
    @step
    async def my_step(self, ev: StartEvent) -> StopEvent:
        return StopEvent(result="Hello, world!")

async def main():
    print(await MyWorkflow(timeout=10, verbose=False).run())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the start and stop

The StartEvent annotation connects the start of the run to my_step. Returning StopEvent(result=...) finishes the run. await ...run() returns its result, which print displays. run(main) supplies the ordinary Python script entry point; this is why no notebook-only top-level await is needed.

Run: python my_workflow.py. Expect Hello, world!. What part used an LLM?

Answer

None. A workflow can organize plain Python operations. An event-driven workflow is not automatically an AI agent.

docs.title: 2. Connect two steps
docs.text:
Follow one message: StartEvent → step_one → ProcessingEvent → step_two → StopEvent. step_one writes “Step 1 complete” into the message. step_two reads that same text and adds “Finished processing:”. The event type connects the steps; Python does not choose the next step just because it is next in the file.

Create my_workflow_steps.py. The first step puts a string into a custom ProcessingEvent. The second step reads it and prints the completed result. It uses no LLM, network or Groq tokens. Follow the event payload between the two methods.

my_workflow_steps.py
from llama_index.core.workflow import Event, StartEvent, StopEvent, Workflow, step
from week05_common import run

class ProcessingEvent(Event):
    intermediate_result: str

class MultiStepWorkflow(Workflow):
    @step
    async def step_one(self, ev: StartEvent) -> ProcessingEvent:
        return ProcessingEvent(intermediate_result="Step 1 complete")

    @step
    async def step_two(self, ev: ProcessingEvent) -> StopEvent:
        return StopEvent(result=f"Finished processing: {ev.intermediate_result}")

async def main():
    print(await MultiStepWorkflow(timeout=10, verbose=False).run())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain event routing

The first step returns a ProcessingEvent, which matches the input annotation of step_two. The intermediate_result field is the data passed between them. The event types connect the steps; their names and placement in the file are not the routing rule.

Run: python my_workflow_steps.py. Expect Finished processing: Step 1 complete.

docs.title: 3. Branch and loop
docs.text:
HF demonstrates a step that can either loop or continue. Here the example loops exactly once so you can predict and inspect both paths. The timeout provides a second bound; do not create an unlimited retry loop.

Create my_workflow_loop.py. It returns a LoopEvent on its first attempt, then a ProcessingEvent that allows the second step to finish. Its input is the initial start event; the event carries the attempt counter. It prints the branch decisions and final result without an LLM or network.

my_workflow_loop.py
from llama_index.core.workflow import Event, StartEvent, StopEvent, Workflow, step
from week05_common import run

class LoopEvent(Event):
    attempt: int

class ProcessingEvent(Event):
    intermediate_result: str

class LoopWorkflow(Workflow):
    @step
    async def step_one(self, ev: StartEvent | LoopEvent) -> ProcessingEvent | LoopEvent:
        attempt = ev.attempt if isinstance(ev, LoopEvent) else 0
        if attempt < 1:
            print("Try again once")
            return LoopEvent(attempt=attempt + 1)
        print("Continue to step two")
        return ProcessingEvent(intermediate_result="First step complete")

    @step
    async def step_two(self, ev: ProcessingEvent) -> StopEvent:
        return StopEvent(result=f"Finished processing: {ev.intermediate_result}")

async def main():
    print(await LoopWorkflow(timeout=10, verbose=False).run())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the loop

StartEvent | LoopEvent means this step accepts either event type. On the first call the attempt is zero. Returning LoopEvent(attempt=1) routes back to the same step; that field prevents another loop. Returning ProcessingEvent takes the other branch and reaches step_two. A loop in a program does not imply an API rate-limit retry.

Predict the output, then run: python my_workflow_loop.py.

Try again once

Finished processing: First step complete

docs.title: 5. Keep shared state with Context
docs.text:
Think of Context as a shared notebook for this workflow run. An event carries a message to a matching step. Context stores information that later steps can look up by name. Here, the program writes a question under the name query, then reads it back. This state is kept in memory for the run; it is not a saved file.

Create my_workflow_state.py. It stores HF’s France-capital question, retrieves the same string in a later step and reads it again after the run. It prints the stored query and a completion message. It does not answer the question, contact an LLM or use Groq tokens.

my_workflow_state.py
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context, Event, StartEvent, StopEvent, Workflow, step
from week05_common import run

class ProcessingEvent(Event):
    intermediate_result: str

class StateWorkflow(Workflow):
    @step
    async def step_one(self, ctx: Context, ev: StartEvent) -> ProcessingEvent:
        await ctx.store.set("query", "What is the capital of France?")
        return ProcessingEvent(intermediate_result="Step 1 complete")

    @step
    async def step_two(self, ctx: Context, ev: ProcessingEvent) -> StopEvent:
        query = await ctx.store.get("query")
        print("STORED QUERY:", query)
        return StopEvent(result=f"Finished processing: {ev.intermediate_result}")

async def main():
    workflow = StateWorkflow(timeout=10, verbose=False)
    ctx = Context(workflow)
    print(await workflow.run(ctx=ctx))
    print("STATE AFTER RUN:", await ctx.store.get("query"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain shared state

ctx.store.set writes a named value; ctx.store.get reads it. Both steps receive the same run context. The final read uses that same context after completion. The ProcessingEvent still routes the workflow; context stores shared information alongside that event flow.

Run: python my_workflow_state.py. Find What is the capital of France? twice. Did any code establish that the answer is Paris?

Answer

No. This program stores and reads a question. It contains no lookup or model operation that answers it. A printed question is not evidence that a task was solved.

docs.title: 6. Automate a team workflow and count calls
docs.text:
Finally HF returns to an agent team: multiplication and addition agents, a root agent and shared state. This connects the workflow ideas to the model-driven decisions from the previous lesson.

Create my_team_workflow.py. It sends HF’s addition question to the multiplication agent first. That agent should hand off to the addition agent, which calls add. The arithmetic tools update a shared counter. It uses Groq tokens and prints the tool trace, final answer and arithmetic-call count.

my_team_workflow.py
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import AgentWorkflow, FunctionAgent
from llama_index.core.workflow import Context
from week05_common import get_llm, run, show_agent

async def add(ctx: Context, a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two integers and count this arithmetic call."""
    state = await ctx.store.get("state")
    state["num_fn_calls"] += 1
    await ctx.store.set("state", state)
    return a + b

async def multiply(ctx: Context, a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiply two integers and count this arithmetic call."""
    state = await ctx.store.get("state")
    state["num_fn_calls"] += 1
    await ctx.store.set("state", state)
    return a * b

async def main():
    llm = get_llm()
    multiplier = FunctionAgent(
        name="multiply_agent", description="Multiplies two integers.", tools=[multiply], llm=llm,
        can_handoff_to=["add_agent"],
        system_prompt="Use multiply for multiplication. Hand all addition requests to add_agent.",
    )
    adder = FunctionAgent(
        name="add_agent", description="Adds two integers.", tools=[add], llm=llm,
        can_handoff_to=["multiply_agent"],
        system_prompt="Use add for addition. Return the result from the tool.",
    )
    workflow = AgentWorkflow(
        agents=[multiplier, adder], root_agent="multiply_agent", timeout=180,
        initial_state={"num_fn_calls": 0},
        state_prompt="Current state: {state}. User message: {msg}",
    )
    ctx = Context(workflow)
    await show_agent(workflow, "Can you add 5 and 3? Hand off to add_agent and use add.", ctx=ctx)
    state = await ctx.store.get("state")
    print("ARITHMETIC CALLS:", state["num_fn_calls"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(main)
Explain the team state

initial_state sets a shared dictionary with a zero count. Each arithmetic tool receives ctx, increments the counter and stores it again. Context is injected by the framework; it is not a number supplied by the model. state_prompt makes the current state available with the user message. Only the arithmetic functions increment this counter: it does not count model requests, handoffs or tokens. This example uses a sequential handoff; concurrent state updates would need additional coordination.

Run: python my_team_workflow.py once.

Check these separately: a handoff to add_agent, an add call with 5 and 3, return value 8, a final answer consistent with 8, and ARITHMETIC CALLS: 1 for one arithmetic call. If the count is greater than one, inspect the trace for repeated arithmetic calls. A count alone does not identify which tool ran or prove the answer is correct.
